PullRequest.Title: build: stop processes that hold Windows test log files before publishing them
PullRequest.Body:
`🔒 Publish Log Files` in the Windows `Browser & Remote Tests` job failed in main CI twice, in [492717](https://dev.azure.com/monacotools/Monaco/_build/results?buildId=492717) and [493303](https://dev.azure.com/monacotools/Monaco/_build/results?buildId=493303). Every test passed. Files under `.build\logs\integration-tests-remote` (`window1\exthost\exthost.log`, `server\agenthost.log`, `remoteagent.log`, …) were still "being used by another process".

## Why the existing kill step doesn't cover it

`Kill lingering test processes` stops processes whose **executable** is under `$(agent.builddirectory)\test`.
- In 493303 it stopped the 3 server `node.exe` processes, but the files were still locked 35 s later.
- In 492717 it found nothing to stop.

So whatever held them runs from somewhere else. The process list from `Diagnostics after smoke test run` shows a lingering **`git.exe`** owned by the build user in **both** failing runs, and in none of the 8 green main runs before 493303. A process started from the server or an extension host (git is started by the Git extension) inherits that process's inheritable file handles, and it can outlive it. I haven't proven that git is the holder, which is why this logs what it finds.

## Fix

- The new `build/azure-pipelines/win32/stop-log-file-holders.ps1` asks the Windows Restart Manager (`RmGetList`) which processes hold any file under `.build\logs`. It logs each one's pid, name, parent, owner, path and command line, and stops it if it belongs to the build user and isn't an `Agent.*` process. It then checks again and logs anything still holding a file.
- The existing kill step calls it after its executable-path loop. The step stays `continueOnError: true`.

## Validation

Locally, with Windows PowerShell 5.1, which the step uses:
- **Nothing holding:** logs `No process holds files`, exit 0.
- **A process holding `exthost.log` exclusively:** `Get-FileHash` failed with "used by another process". The script named the holder with its command line and stopped it, and then the hash succeeded.
- **The CI shape:** a parent opened `server\remoteagent.log` with an inheritable handle, started `ping.exe`, and exited. The orphaned `ping.exe` held the file. The script found it by file, logged `parent=<dead pid>`, and stopped it, and then the file opened exclusively.
- **Missing folder:** exit 0.

Proof: def 111 CI build, Windows x64 only, Publish off: [493385](https://dev.azure.com/monacotools/Monaco/_build/results?buildId=493385). It checks that the step runs on the agent and logs its result there.

> Authored with Copilot

Scenarios.Scenario: Normal Windows product-test job finalization with no process holding a log file
Scenarios.CriticalPath: After tests and result publication, the existing broad process cleanup runs, then the new script synchronously compiles its Restart Manager interop helper, recursively enumerates `.build/logs`, and—when files exist—completes one Restart Manager session before the always-on pipeline artifact upload can begin. All added work is on job-finalization's critical path.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Dynamically compile and load the C# Restart Manager interop type with `Add-Type`.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Once per Windows product-test job because the script runs in its own PowerShell task.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The previous cleanup was inline PowerShell and performed no dynamic compilation.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Must complete before holder detection and therefore before job-finalization artifact publication.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Recursively enumerate every file under `.build/logs` and materialize each full path.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One directory traversal and F path objects when no holder is found.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The previous cleanup did not traverse the log tree; the later artifact publisher still performed its own unchanged traversal/upload.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Synchronous prerequisite to the Restart Manager query and subsequent artifact publication.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Start a Restart Manager session, bulk-register F files, query affected processes, and end the session.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One session with one bulk registration and one `RmGetList` probe in the no-holder case, independent of F call count.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No Restart Manager boundary existed; cleanup only queried the process list and killed executables rooted under the test directory.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The native OS query completes synchronously before publication can proceed.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Publish `.build/logs` as the pipeline log artifact.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One artifact publication per job, with uploaded bytes/files determined by the existing log tree.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same artifact was always published immediately after the prior cleanup and remaining job steps.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: This unchanged post-job output now starts after the new cleanup script; the diff does not increase upload cardinality or bytes.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: The number F of files recursively present under `.build/logs`; the helper materializes F full paths and registers all F in one bulk Restart Manager call. Effective holder cardinality is zero in this scenario.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Fully serialized in one PowerShell task. File enumeration is sequential from the caller's perspective, and all F paths are grouped into one Restart Manager registration rather than F calls. No limiter is needed because there is one session and no per-file concurrency.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: There is no cross-job cache: this task starts a fresh Windows PowerShell process, so `Add-Type` runs once per job. File paths and the negative no-holder result are not cached, but in the no-holder branch they are computed only once. The existing artifact publisher later traverses the directory independently.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the changed YAML unconditionally invokes the script under `condition: always()`, and the script's compile, recursive enumeration, and bulk native call are explicit. There is no per-file boundary fan-out.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Repository evidence does not establish typical F or measured `Add-Type`/Restart Manager duration. The work runs once at job teardown, is bulked, and does not execute in an interactive or repeated test path.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression. The diff adds bounded, synchronous teardown overhead, but groups all files into one Restart Manager registration and performs only one scan/query on the dominant no-holder path; there is no high-confidence hot-path, fan-out, or unbounded mechanism.

Scenarios.Scenario: Windows product-test job finalization when one or more out-of-tree processes hold log files
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The same compile, recursive scan, and Restart Manager query run first. For each of H unique holders, the task synchronously queries WMI metadata/ownership, may force-stop the process, waits up to 10 seconds for that process, then performs one second full log-tree scan and Restart Manager session. Artifact publication waits for all of this.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Recursively enumerate all log files before and after holder cleanup.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Two traversals, materializing F paths each time, regardless of how many files each holder has open.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The prior cleanup did not inspect log files or re-scan them after process termination.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Both synchronous traversals precede artifact publication; the second verifies cleanup.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Run two bulk Restart Manager sessions to discover holders before cleanup and verify remaining holders afterward.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Two sessions, each with one bulk F-file registration; holder results are deduplicated before per-process handling.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No file-holder query existed, so out-of-tree holders survived and could cause the later publication to fail.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Both OS queries block cleanup completion and artifact publication.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Query `Win32_Process` and invoke `GetOwner` for each unique holder through CIM/WMI.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Up to two serialized WMI operations per unique holder PID H.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The existing cleanup made one broad `Win32_Process` query and filtered by executable path; it did not perform per-holder lookup/owner calls for out-of-tree processes.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Ownership and agent-process checks must finish before each stop decision.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Force-stop each eligible holder and wait up to 10 seconds for termination.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most one stop and one serialized wait per eligible unique holder; ineligible/current/agent holders are skipped.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Only processes whose executable path was under the test root were stopped, without an explicit wait; out-of-tree holders such as inherited `git.exe` processes were not touched.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Termination and any wait directly delay the artifact upload, but remove the file lock that previously caused publication failure.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Publish `.build/logs` as a pipeline artifact after cleanup.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One unchanged artifact upload per job.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Publication could begin sooner but fail when an out-of-tree process retained a log handle.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The upload is delayed by holder cleanup but is expected to succeed after locks are released instead of failing on locked files.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: F log files and H unique holder PIDs returned after `Sort-Object -Unique`; WMI and stop/wait work scales with H, while filesystem/native registration work is exactly two bulk passes when any holder is detected.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Holder processing is deliberately serial. There is no concurrent process-stop burst; each eligible holder is stopped and awaited before the next. Restart Manager still receives files in one bulk call per pass.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No positive or negative holder cache is retained. The second enumeration/query intentionally refreshes state after stopping processes. PID deduplication prevents repeated per-holder WMI/stop work when one process holds multiple files.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: F- and H-scaling, PID deduplication, serial waits, and the second verification pass are explicit in changed code. The task is directly before post-job artifact publication.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The repository and PR metadata establish rare observed holder incidents and examples with a small number of processes, but do not establish large H, large F, or force-killed processes routinely consuming the full wait timeout. Thus the theoretical O(F + H) teardown delay lacks a realistic high-impact trigger.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression. The extra work is intentional, holder-triggered teardown on the publication critical path; file operations are bulked, holder PIDs are deduplicated, and process handling is serialized. There is insufficient evidence of realistically large H/F or repeated 10-second waits to establish an actionable performance bug.

Analysis.Summary: Reviewed the complete two-file diff and traced normal and holder-present Windows CI teardown paths through dynamic compilation, filesystem traversal, Restart Manager, WMI, process termination, and artifact publication. The PR adds bounded one-time cleanup latency but avoids per-file boundary fan-out and concurrency bursts; no high-confidence performance regression or qualifying regression fix was found.
